title: Complaint to Product
goal: Your kid designs a product for someone else's problem, not their own. They collect complaints from real people, find the one that keeps coming up, build a rough model from cardboard, watch the people who complained try it, then fix it and find out if anyone would really choose it.
need: A few people to listen to: family, friends, neighbours
A notebook for their exact words
Time to go back and test

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: You don't need to be handy or creative. You're the first person they interview and the ride to the others. Your most useful question is 'Who's it for?' Keep bringing them back to the people who complained, especially when they fall in love with their own idea.

plan.what: Collect complaints and find the pattern (Steps 1 and 2).
Invent it and build a rough model (Step 3).
Test it, fix it and ask for a real yes (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: They only want to invent for themselves
troubleshoot.a: Fair, and Problem-Solver Studio is made for that. Here, ask: 'Who else has this problem? Let's go and ask them.'

troubleshoot.q: People are too polite to criticize
troubleshoot.a: Ask them to show you, not tell you. Watching someone use it is honest even when people are being nice.
Good, that's what models are for. Ask which part broke first, and rebuild only that part.

lesson.text: A good product doesn't start with an idea. It starts with listening to someone else's complaint, and it isn't finished until they'd actually choose it.
lesson.before: I'll invent a backpack with a built-in snack fridge.

model.line: Four people said their charger cord keeps falling behind the table.
It slides off every time the phone is unplugged.
A clip with a cardboard weight that keeps the end on the table.
Three of four used it without help, and two asked for one of their own.

lesson.modelNote: The snack fridge fixed a problem only your kid had. The clip came from listening, and the test showed it works for other people.

steps.title: Collect complaints
steps.why: Every product you own started as someone's complaint.
steps.kid: Your kid asks at least five people about one part of their day, like getting out the door, meals, trips or chores, using the Listening questions card in the Product Toolkit at the end of the guide. They write down people's exact words, not just the gist.
steps.you: Be the practice interview and give real answers. Then help them reach people outside the family, like a friend's parent, a coach or a neighbour, and stay nearby while they ask.
ask: What did they say, word for word?
What do they do about it right now?
steps.tip: 'Tell me about your mornings' gets far more than 'What bugs you?' People complain freely once they're telling a story.

levels.explore: Ask two people to tell you about their mornings, and draw what they said.
levels.develop: Ask five people about one part of the day and write their exact words.
levels.extend: Ask eight people of different ages, and note who complained most and about what.

steps.title: Find the pattern
steps.why: One complaint is a story. The same one three times is a product.
steps.kid: Your kid spreads out the notes and groups complaints that are really the same problem, using the Spot the pattern card. They pick the one that came up most or bothers people most, and write it in one sentence: who has it, when, and what they do now.
steps.you: Ask 'Who's it for?' until the answer is a real person, not 'everyone'.
ask: Which complaint came up more than once?
What are people already doing to get around it?
steps.tip: Workarounds are gold. If someone's already using an elastic and a clothespin to fix it, they really want it fixed.

levels.explore: Find two complaints that are really the same problem, and pick one.
levels.develop: Group every complaint, and write the top one in a sentence.
levels.extend: Rank the top three by how often and how much they bother people, and defend your pick.

steps.title: Invent it and build a rough model
steps.why: A cardboard model answers questions a drawing can't.
steps.kid: Your kid sketches a few ways to fix it, picks one and builds a rough model from cardboard, tape and whatever's around, using the Make it real card. They label what each part does.
steps.you: Ask 'How would they hold it?' and 'Where would it live?' Help with the cutting, and leave the design to them. If they get stuck, ask what the person does now and build one small step up from that.
ask: How would they use it on a busy day?
What's the one part it can't do without?
steps.tip: Ugly is fine. A model has one job, and that's to be tested.

levels.explore: Draw your invention with labels, then build one part of it from cardboard.
levels.develop: Build a rough model that shows how it works.
levels.extend: Build two different models, and plan how to find out which one people prefer.

steps.title: Watch them use it
steps.why: People will say they love it. Watch what their hands do.
steps.kid: Your kid takes the model back to the people who complained and hands it over without explaining. They watch, using the Test it card: where people get stuck, what they try first and what they say. Then they ask what they'd change.
steps.you: Go with them, and stay quiet while the person tries it. Afterwards, ask your kid what surprised them.
ask: Would they swap what they do now for this?
steps.tip: Don't explain it first. If it needs explaining, that's the most useful thing you'll learn.

levels.explore: Show one person your model and ask what they think.
levels.develop: Test it with three people without explaining, and write down where they got stuck.
levels.extend: Test both models with the same people, and count which one they choose.

steps.title: Fix it and ask for a real yes
steps.why: The only test that counts: would they choose it?
steps.kid: Your kid changes the model based on what they saw, then gives it a name and a price. They go back and ask the real question: would you pay for this, or swap it for what you use now? Then they fill in My product at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Help them hear a no as information, not a verdict. Ask what would turn it into a yes.
ask: What would change a no into a yes?
steps.tip: 'I'd buy that' is polite. 'Can I have one when it's ready?' is a real yes.

levels.explore: Make one change, and ask one person if they'd use it.
levels.develop: Make two changes, name it, price it and ask three people for a real yes.
levels.extend: Work out what one would cost to make, and whether people's price would cover it.

conclusion.headline: They made something for someone else, and checked that it worked.
conclusion.text: Notice how they react the next time someone grumbles. If they ask 'What do you do about it now?' instead of rolling their eyes, they're designing for other people.
conclusion.celebrate: When someone uses the thing they made, say: 'You listened to them, and it shows.'
extensions: Run the same listening on a different part of the day, like bedtime
Build the next model from a different material
Design the packaging and the one sentence that would sell it
Show your model to someone who makes things for a living, and ask what they'd change

signs: They ask people questions before they start building
They notice the workarounds people use
They test ideas on someone else
makeItReal: Keep a complaints page in a notebook. When the same one shows up three times, it's time for a new model.

onTheRoad: Spot three clever workarounds people use here, like how they carry, shade or store things, and guess the complaint behind each.
Build a rough fix for your family's biggest travel annoyance, like a bag strap or a lost charger, from whatever you can find.
With your help, ask a market seller or your host what bugs them most in their day, and compare it with complaints from home.
backHome: Bring one workaround you saw on the road home as a rough model, and test it on a complaint someone there keeps making.
